definition: Sacrosanct means holy; too important to be criticized or interfered with.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word sacrosanct. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know sacrosanct should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The studio's master tapes were sacrosanct: engineers copied them once, then locked the originals away from every producer's 'quick fix.'
Respected stops short of sacrosanct — what is respected gets a hearing and consideration, nothing more.
Sacred stops short of sacrosanct — the sacred is revered, but the sacrosanct is fenced: criticism itself trespasses.

Inviolable marks a line that must never be crossed, protection stated as law or principle — an inviolable right, an inviolable border. Sacrosanct wraps the same protection in reverence: the thing is fenced off because it is treated as holy, so even questioning it feels like trespass.

Untouchable states the bare outcome — no one may interfere — whatever the reason: power, fear, or law. Sacrosanct supplies a particular reason: protection carried by reverence for the thing's importance. A monopoly shielded by sheer market power is untouchable; no one calls it sacrosanct.

Sacrosanct means holy; too important to be criticized or interfered with.
Every March the botany department defends its seed vault budget as sacrosanct — heat, light, and payroll have all been cut in lean years, but no dean has ever touched the vault.

Sacrosanct began as literal law — Rome's sacrosanct officials were 'made holy' so that harming them was sacrilege — and the word still means protection raised to the level of taboo: what is sacrosanct isn't just valued, it is off-limits even to argument.

Sacrosanct does most of its modern work outside religion, usually with one eyebrow raised: budgets, rituals, and parking spots get called sacrosanct precisely when someone thinks the protection is excessive.
For sincere reverence, say sacred; for bureaucratic untouchability, sacrosanct.

For a hundred and six years, seniors at Harwick College have rung the chapel bell by hand at dawn on the first day of exams.
When a new provost suggested a recording — the rope was fraying, and dawn shifts were hard to fill — the reaction startled her.
Alumni wrote furious letters.
The student paper ran the headline 'Some Things Are Not Up for Discussion.' One trustee walked out of the meeting where the idea was raised.
No rule protected the bell.
What protected it, the provost realized, was reverence: the ringing was sacrosanct, and even floating the question read as a kind of trespass.
She withdrew the proposal, budgeted for a new rope, and took the dawn shift herself that spring.
